action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_scrape
tools.description: Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state. `firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call. Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_search
tools.description: Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation. `developer` returns hits in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`; the other categories also filter `data.web`.

## 598adf58-4d0d-4866-82b2-42a10512e240

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application. Finder is an application like any other: clicking the desktop, the Dock, or a Finder window (including Go to Folder) requires a Finder grant. The menu bar does not, as long as the app that is frontmost is one you already have access to.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application. Finder is an application like any other: clicking the desktop, the Dock, or a Finder window (including Go to Folder) requires a Finder grant. The menu bar does not, as long as the app that is frontmost is one you already have access to.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

177	## Tensions and contradictions
178	
179	1. **The task's own premise doesn't fully hold.** Both class transcripts (Class 1 and Class 3) are diarized entirely under a single Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line — including Class 3, which the Spring 2026 teaching schedule assigns solo to Rash (`spring-2026-teaching.md`: "Feb. 5 | Conditioning - Alactic-Aerobic | Rash"). Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name instead of doing real per-speaker diarization. This means roughly 30,000 words of the richest, most first-person material in this corpus cannot be confidently attributed to Rash specifically versus Ruf or Wenger. Every transcript-sourced bullet above is marked Inferred for this reason, even where the underlying statement is a confident, first-person claim.
180	
181	2. **Department reporting model is not internally consistent.** The Playbook (p.6) frames Applied Performance as a peer discipline inside Health & Wellness that "enables" Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Nutrition, and Mental Health to answer their own questions. But Week 1 course material lists "Applied Performance" as one of many training sub-categories nested under Athletic Performance itself (p.11), and the same transcript narration describes Rash's role as "helping program and plan the training" — a support-staff framing, not a peer-department framing. Which model actually governs day-to-day authority is not reconciled anywhere in these documents.
182	
183	3. **Coach's-eye-first versus objective-first is argued both ways.** The course material repeatedly argues that "you don't need a fancy test... you have to have a good coach's eye" and criticizes the GPS/load-monitoring era for breeding a fear-driven under-training culture. Eric's own SportSmith writing moves the opposite direction on daily monitoring specifically: he replaced subjective wellness surveys with objective force-plate mRSI because subjective self-report couldn't be trusted. Both share a skepticism of trendy or convenient data, but they land on opposite defaults (trust the trained eye vs. require an objective number) for the daily-monitoring question specifically.
184	
185	4. **The Assessment Manual (V12) reads as an older document than the current technology stack.** It builds its 1RM-estimation protocol around GymAware, and its CMJ description references a "contact mat" for jump height. The current Playbook technology stack and the Development Plan both center velocity-based training on Perch, not GymAware, and the current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol runs all CMJ variants exclusively on ForceDecks force plates, with no contact mat mentioned. This suggests the Assessment Manual predates the current VALD/Perch-centered stack and may be a legacy document rather than the currently operative protocol — worth confirming directly with Eric before treating any of its specifics as current practice.
186	
187	5. **Testing cueing instructions conflict across two protocol documents for the same test.** The Assessment Manual's CMJ instructions say explicitly: "Do not coach the strategy of jumping." The current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol gives testers specific verbal cues to give athletes during CMJ, squat-jump, and hop-test administration ("keep chest up," "land softly," "land stiff-legged on only the toes"). These may be reconcilable (safety/technique cues vs. jump-strategy cues are different things), but the two documents read differently on how much a tester should say out loud.
188	
189	6. **Two different anaerobic-threshold heart-rate methods appear back to back in the same slide deck without being reconciled.** One slide gives an age-based formula (max HR = 220-age for men, 226-age for women, threshold at ~85% of that), and the very next slides give a body-size-based table (big/medium/small athlete, ~165/170/175 bpm threshold) as the operational standard used elsewhere throughout the conditioning material. Which one is actually used day to day is not stated. [class-4-2026.md pp.27-29]
190	
191	7. **The Development Plan's own critique cuts against the corpus it's part of.** It states the current Baylor Playbook "has no educational component whatsoever" and reads "like a vendor product reference manual," even though Eric personally co-teaches a full graduate-level course covering much of the same material the Playbook is missing. The department's teaching capacity clearly exists; it just hasn't been captured back into the Playbook or a formal intern curriculum yet.
192	
193	8. **The Playbook's NordBord documentation has not caught up with practice.** The Playbook's Technology Overview and Workflows still document a full, unqualified, roster-style NordBord data-collection SOP. The SportSmith piece describes explicitly retiring roster-wide NordBord testing for football starting after January 2023, keeping it only for small, targeted return-to-play groups. The written SOP has not been updated to reflect that decision.
194	
195	9. **A personally-stated periodization preference is stated inside an unreliable-speaker transcript.** "For me personally, this is a more preferential model to use" (about undulating over linear periodization) is a strong, direct, first-person preference claim — but it comes from the same unreliably-diarized Class 1 transcript described in Tension 1, so it cannot be confirmed as Eric's own stated preference without his direct confirmation.
196	
197	10. **Older vs. current unit-goal templates show almost no adopted content.** The Geyer and Skodinski Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are staff-authored templates for individual sport programming philosophy; Geyer's is mostly filled in (periodization model, weekly split, KPI tests for softball), Skodinski's is nearly blank (just the section headers). Neither is attributed to Eric, and there's no equivalent document in this corpus showing Eric's own answers to the same template questions — a real gap if Flint wants Eric's own unit-goal-style programming philosophy in his own words.

---
type: video-summary
video_id: TIRINmtZOu0
title: "SSAC19: Training Schedule Confounds the Relationship between Acute Chronic Workload Ratio and Injury"
event: SSAC19 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Luke Bourne (caption spelling), Patrick Ward]
topics: [sports-science, injury-health, american-football, other-sport:soccer, decision-making]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

The speakers argue that the published link between the acute chronic workload ratio (ACWR) and injury may be a statistical artifact of the training schedule. A hard recent week makes a hard session today more likely, and the intensity of that session is what raises injury risk. They simulated seasons from NFL and Italian soccer load data in which only same-session intensity affected injury, and the ACWR still looked strongly predictive. When session load is accounted for, ACWR loses significance in their data. They say this does not prove the earlier papers wrong. It matters because the metric underpins software and consulting products sold as injury prevention.

## Key claims

- The first speaker says a vendor once claimed it could cut injury rates by over 50%, and he calls that claim false; he is generally skeptical of injury-prevention products. [00:30]
- ACWR is the last 7 days of load divided by the last 28 days, and it has been applied to many load types, including perceived exertion, heart rate, GPS, accelerometer data and minutes played. [04:35]
- The literature proposes a U-shaped relationship with injury and a "sweet spot" of lower risk. [05:05]
- Positives named for ACWR: easy to calculate, intuitive for coaches, and it pushes coaches to consider past training and not only today. [05:36]
- The speakers say critics had already raised other problems: exponentially weighted versions, mathematical coupling of numerator and denominator, weak out-of-sample prediction, and no data in the offseason. [08:09]
- The speakers' hunch was that ACWR is an artifact of the training schedule, because training camp has both the highest load and the highest injury risk. [09:39]
- Prior studies calculate ACWR going into each session and check whether an injury occurred in that session; they find a strong relationship across sports. [10:40]
- The proposed causal structure: schedule drives both ACWR and session intensity, and session intensity drives injury. A hard prior week predicts a hard upcoming session. [11:41]
- In the speakers' own data, ACWR is highly predictive of injury in a given session. [13:12]
- In simulations where ACWR had no effect by construction, ACWR still came out extremely significant on a chi-square test. [14:13]
- The apparent injury-risk increase in the simulations was about the same order as the literature reports. [15:15]
- Sessions in the "danger zone" of ACWR were more likely to be hard sessions. [16:16]
- A suggested fix is to use the actual session load of the session in which injury occurred, for example with survival models, latent variable models, or other players' loads in the same session. [17:49]
- Prior studies have not used same-session load because the data for an injured player is usually discarded. [17:18]
- Once session load is accounted for, ACWR goes from highly significant to non-significant in all their cases. [18:19]
- The speakers say they have not disproved the field, only shown the analysis is open to confounding; a more complex model might still find real signal. [18:49] [23:35]

## Numbers and definitions

- ACWR: acute load (most recent 7 days) divided by chronic load (previous 28 days). [04:04]
- Sweet spot: captions read "08 and 1.3", almost certainly 0.8 to 1.3, but the captions do not confirm it. [05:36]
- 2014 first paper (cricket bowlers) cited over 250 times; the 2015 editorial (captions: "blanch and gabbit") cited over 150 times. [07:38]
- Uncoupled ACWR: most recent 7 days over the 28 days before those 7 days. [08:39]
- Data: one NFL team and one Italian soccer team (captions say "Syria" and "Serria", likely Serie A; not confirmed). [12:11]
- Simulation: 1,000 simulated seasons per sport, injury probability depends only on the current session's intensity. [13:43]
- Post-simulation apparent risk increase: 6.8% for the Italian team, 10.5% for the NFL team. The talk does not say whether these are relative or absolute. [15:15]
- Injury definition (Q&A): non-contact injury causing the player to miss a subsequent session or match, in line with the UEFA definition. [20:22] [20:53]
- The 6.8% and 10.5% figures and the session-count claims are read from auto captions; they were not checked against the slides.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Directed acyclic graph of ACWR, schedule, session intensity and injury. [11:10]
- Null-model simulation: simulate season-by-season session injuries where only session load matters, then test ACWR against injury with a chi-square test. [13:43] [14:43]
- Adjustment options: survival models, latent variable models, or predicting the upcoming session load as an unmeasured confounder. [18:19] [25:11]
- Comparison of coupled and uncoupled ACWR denominators, same result. [26:42]

## Limits and open questions

- Two teams from two sports; no detail on roster size, number of injuries, or load metric used.
- Details of the real-data adjustment models are "in the paper" and were not shown. [17:49]
- The talk does not show the adjusted effect sizes, only that significance disappears.
- Whether chronic load is protective is explicitly not addressed. [26:42]
- Whether a richer multivariate model finds signal is left open. [23:35]
- The claim that better sensors would make the problem worse is the speaker's intuition, not a test. [21:54]
- The speakers' view that ACWR products are "snake oil" is their own opinion, stated early in the talk. [01:01]
- Wellness questionnaire data: one speaker says across four sports the players mostly enter the same value (captions: "seven") every day. This is his experience, not a study. [24:39]
- Minor inconsistency: the talk opens strongly against the industry but closes saying it has not disproved the literature. [18:49]

## Q&A

- How is injury defined, and are non-training injuries dropped? Non-contact injuries causing a missed session or match; cannot rule out training relation for off-field injuries. [20:22]
- Do device sensitivity limits matter? Noise in load sensors should weaken the effect, so the speaker expects better data not to remove the problem. [21:23]
- How should decision makers avoid snake oil? Much sport science is well supported (nutrition, strength and conditioning); this may not be one of them. [22:33]
- Could wellness, physiological and biomarker data in a multivariate model do better? Possibly; dose is measurable, response is not well measured, and wellness forms lack validation. [23:35] [24:39]
- Can you predict today's load from the prior 7 days? If so, treat it as an unmeasured confounder and adjust; needs statistical skill. [25:11]
- Do high vs low chronic loads differ, and is chronic load protective? Same results using acute load alone; protection not addressed; coupled and uncoupled denominators gave the same results. [26:42]

## Where this applies

- Inference: Any Baylor football dashboard that flags players by ACWR on Catapult player load, or by a similar 7-to-28-day ratio, should be treated as a description of recent load and schedule, not as an injury-risk score. Check whether the flags mostly fire on the same weeks (camp, return from breaks) for every player.
- Inference: When reviewing a non-contact injury, pull that day's planned session load (or the practice script intensity) next to the prior-week ratio before attributing it to "spike" in load. The talk's point is that the current session's intensity may carry the signal.
- Inference: For Baylor's own retrospective analysis, log planned session intensity as a field so injured-session data is not lost. The talk says the injured player's session data is usually thrown out. [17:18]
- Inference: Use the simulation idea as a test of any internal risk model: simulate seasons where only session intensity matters and see whether the model still "finds" an ACWR effect.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: No formal injury-risk model such as ACWR is attributed to Eric in the corpus; ACWR appears only in Clemson reference material. The talk neither conflicts with nor changes a stated Baylor position.
- Eric's baseline: Abrupt, large changes in volume and intensity are treated as an injury-risk driver, and progressions are kept smooth (course material, speaker unconfirmed, tagged Inferred). The talk agrees that load change matters but says the ratio may just reflect the schedule; it leaves open whether spikes themselves cause injury.
- Eric's baseline: Subjective daily wellness surveys were abandoned because athletes learned to give consistent low-effort answers (Explicit, SportSmith piece). The talk agrees: a speaker describes athletes entering the same number every day. [24:39]

## What would have to be true

- Session-level load (planned and actual) for every player and session, including the session where an injury occurs.
- A clear non-contact injury definition (the talk uses missed session or match).
- Enough injuries and seasons at Baylor to fit a model that includes session load; the talk does not give a minimum, and one college roster may be too small.
- Someone with the statistical training to run survival or latent variable models. The speaker says this takes "fair bit" of skill. [25:41]

## Do not apply when

- You would use the talk to say ACWR-style monitoring is useless. The speakers say they did not disprove it, and do not show that chronic load is non-protective. [18:49] [26:42]
- Your data has only a handful of injuries; a null result then says little.
- The injury is contact-related; the talk's definition excludes it.
- You want to generalize from one NFL team and one Italian soccer team to a college football roster with different schedules and session structure.
- The claim is being used as settled in a staff meeting. It is a conference research talk; the adjusted results were not shown.

## First step

Export one season of Catapult session load and injury dates for football, and count how many non-contact injuries had a recorded session load for that day. If the count is near zero, fix the logging before any modeling.

- Inference: Send results to coaches the same day they are collected, through a fixed channel, so they can plan the week.

- Eric's baseline: Injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, in collaboration with Athletic Medicine (course material, tagged Inferred). The talk agrees: risk, not prediction.

Write a one-page definition for Baylor football: which non-contact injuries count, the outcome measure (missed practices or games), and the test day for each weekly check. Review it with Athletic Medicine before any modeling.

title: "SSAC26: Heat Safety in Professional Sport: Aligning Data Physiology and Policy"
event: SSAC26 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [David Martin]
topics: [american-football, sports-science, injury-health, policy, competitive-advantage]

caption_source: auto
status: draft

## Summary

The speaker, introduced as director of science at Perry Weather, argues that exertional heat illness is preventable and that wet bulb globe temperature (WBGT) monitoring can guide when teams practice, how they acclimatize and what conditions to prepare for. He reviews heat stroke deaths in football, heat acclimation physiology, policy changes in Georgia, and his own look at historical WBGT data from NFL stadium sensors. He also reports a penalty-count difference when WBGT was above 60 F. The company sells environmental monitoring hardware, which he discloses, and the penalty analysis is preliminary.

## Key claims

- Exertional heat stroke is still the leading preventable cause of death in sport. [02:03] [02:33]
- Heat degrades aerobic performance and raises core temperature and heart rate; chronic exposure builds resilience. [02:03]
- Among 61 heat stroke fatalities in one study, all occurred in conditioning drills and not games, most were linemen. [03:35]
- Mapping cases by WBGT lets organizations build policy and best practice. [04:05]
- A chamber study of the Guardian Cap found no significant core temperature difference with or without it. [04:36] [05:06]
- Some athletes in the simulated practice reached core temperatures above 102 F by 39 minutes and 104 F by 75 minutes. [05:06]
- Heat acclimation improves thermal regulation and lowers heat illness risk; a protocol clamps core temperature near 101.3 F for an hour, five times in eight days. [06:09] [06:40]
- Adaptations such as lower heart rate and larger plasma volume peak around day five to six. [07:43] [08:13]
- Acclimating with exercise in a chamber gave a larger effect than passive exposure (Army work, per the speaker). [09:13]
- Heart rate rises with body mass lost to sweat, and sweating impairs. [09:43]
- First heat exposure cut cycling time trial power about 20%, with recovery after repeated exposures. [10:14]
- WBGT combines air temperature, radiant heat, humidity and air movement and is the standard heat stress metric in the military and many sports bodies. [10:44] [11:16]
- Georgia modification policies (clothing, practice duration) reduced heat illness. [11:46] [12:16]
- Sensor data at Jacksonville's stadium on the hottest day suggested a practice window of 6 a.m. to noon. [12:46] [13:17]
- Heat exposure should not be avoided entirely because it drives acclimation. [13:47]
- August is when most heat illness happens, after athletes return unconditioned. [14:17]
- WBGT above 60 F was associated with about 2.7 more penalties per game; the signal was stronger in the second half. [17:20] [17:51]
- The speaker interprets this as heat raising fatigue and irritability; another study found the pattern only for home teams. [18:21] [18:51]
- Proposed protocol: practice in the cooler window, then do passive acclimation at the end with cold tubs and supervision. [19:22]

## Numbers and definitions

- 159 exertional heat stroke deaths from 1980 to 2009 in youth, high school and college players. [03:04]
- 61 fatalities: 100% in conditioning drills, 97% linemen, 37% "punished by exercise" (caption spelling). [03:35]
- Heat stroke in the field is usually core temperature above 104 F with central nervous system dysfunction; highest he has seen was 112 F (survived). [05:38]
- Acclimation protocol: jog 15 to 20 minutes to 101.3 F, hold one hour, five sessions in eight days. [06:40]
- 1940s study: 45 men, 9 kg load, 20 km in 50 C; half had heat sickness day one, none by day five. [07:11]
- Heart rate rises 3 to 5 beats per minute for each 1% body mass lost through sweat. [09:43]
- Core temperature rise per 1% body mass is captioned "27 to 36 degrees Fahrenheit", which is not plausible as stated and is likely garbled. [09:43]
- About 20% lower cycling power on first heat exposure. [10:14]
- Georgia policy drop in heat illness is captioned "30 to 100%"; the real figure is unclear. [12:16]
- Company: about 6,000 hardware units across the US since 2012, 16 at NFL stadiums. [01:00] [12:46]
- July 2025: 159 hours above 87 F in the Jacksonville data (same number as the deaths count, may be coincidence or caption error). [14:47]
- WBGT reached about 90 at some stadiums; season average 60 to 65 F. [16:20] [16:50]
- Penalty analysis: WBGT above 60 F, +2.7 penalties per game; second half +1.5 (direction only). [17:20] [17:51]

## Methods and frameworks named

- WBGT from three sensors: shielded air temperature, black globe, natural wet bulb. [11:16]
- Chamber protocols for acclimation and for equipment testing. [04:36] [06:40]
- Area under the curve of rectal temperature and heart rate to gauge acclimation. [08:43]
- Matching stadium sensor data to game data to compare penalties. [17:20]
- Practice-window analysis from hourly WBGT by month. [13:17] [14:47]

## Limits and open questions

- The speaker works for a company that sells WBGT hardware and alerts; the conclusions favor monitoring. [01:00]
- Penalty analysis: league, seasons, number of games and statistical tests not stated; he says most games were neither very hot nor cold. [17:51]
- "Directionally higher" second-half result is not a tested effect. [17:51]
- The behavior mechanism (heat plus fatigue plus adrenaline) is his interpretation. [18:21] [18:51]
- The 61-fatality statistics cover a specific study and population; the ages and era are not given for that set.
- State policy examples (Texas) are for secondary schools, not college or NFL. [13:17] [13:47]
- Many captions are garbled (names, units); see numbers.
- The speaker has not analyzed position-specific risk yet. [20:53]

## Q&A

- Does Perry Weather work with apparel brands on clothing for specific temperatures? Not at Perry; his institute has done vest and backpack-venting tests in the chamber. [21:55]
- Has he studied cold acclimation for winter sports? Not at his institute; points to an Army researcher (captions: "John Castellani"). [22:25] [22:56]

---
type: video-summary
video_id: TIRINmtZOu0
title: "SSAC19: Training Schedule Confounds the Relationship between Acute Chronic Workload Ratio and Injury"
event: SSAC19 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Luke Bourne (caption spelling), Patrick Ward]
topics: [sports-science, injury-health, american-football, other-sport:soccer, decision-making]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

The speakers argue that the published link between the acute chronic workload ratio (ACWR) and injury may be a statistical artifact of the training schedule. A hard recent week makes a hard session today more likely, and the intensity of that session is what raises injury risk. They simulated seasons from NFL and Italian soccer load data in which only same-session intensity affected injury, and the ACWR still looked strongly predictive. When session load is accounted for, ACWR loses significance in their data. They say this does not prove the earlier papers wrong. It matters because the metric underpins software and consulting products sold as injury prevention.

## Key claims

- The first speaker says a vendor once claimed it could cut injury rates by over 50%, and he calls that claim false; he is generally skeptical of injury-prevention products. [00:30]
- ACWR is the last 7 days of load divided by the last 28 days, and it has been applied to many load types, including perceived exertion, heart rate, GPS, accelerometer data and minutes played. [04:35]
- The literature proposes a U-shaped relationship with injury and a "sweet spot" of lower risk. [05:05]
- Positives named for ACWR: easy to calculate, intuitive for coaches, and it pushes coaches to consider past training and not only today. [05:36]
- The speakers say critics had already raised other problems: exponentially weighted versions, mathematical coupling of numerator and denominator, weak out-of-sample prediction, and no data in the offseason. [08:09]
- The speakers' hunch was that ACWR is an artifact of the training schedule, because training camp has both the highest load and the highest injury risk. [09:39]
- Prior studies calculate ACWR going into each session and check whether an injury occurred in that session; they find a strong relationship across sports. [10:40]
- The proposed causal structure: schedule drives both ACWR and session intensity, and session intensity drives injury. A hard prior week predicts a hard upcoming session. [11:41]
- In the speakers' own data, ACWR is highly predictive of injury in a given session. [13:12]
- In simulations where ACWR had no effect by construction, ACWR still came out extremely significant on a chi-square test. [14:13]
- The apparent injury-risk increase in the simulations was about the same order as the literature reports. [15:15]
- Sessions in the "danger zone" of ACWR were more likely to be hard sessions. [16:16]
- A suggested fix is to use the actual session load of the session in which injury occurred, for example with survival models, latent variable models, or other players' loads in the same session. [17:49]
- Prior studies have not used same-session load because the data for an injured player is usually discarded. [17:18]
- Once session load is accounted for, ACWR goes from highly significant to non-significant in all their cases. [18:19]
- The speakers say they have not disproved the field, only shown the analysis is open to confounding; a more complex model might still find real signal. [18:49] [23:35]

## Numbers and definitions

- ACWR: acute load (most recent 7 days) divided by chronic load (previous 28 days). [04:04]
- Sweet spot: captions read "08 and 1.3", almost certainly 0.8 to 1.3, but the captions do not confirm it. [05:36]
- 2014 first paper (cricket bowlers) cited over 250 times; the 2015 editorial (captions: "blanch and gabbit") cited over 150 times. [07:38]
- Uncoupled ACWR: most recent 7 days over the 28 days before those 7 days. [08:39]
- Data: one NFL team and one Italian soccer team (captions say "Syria" and "Serria", likely Serie A; not confirmed). [12:11]
- Simulation: 1,000 simulated seasons per sport, injury probability depends only on the current session's intensity. [13:43]
- Post-simulation apparent risk increase: 6.8% for the Italian team, 10.5% for the NFL team. The talk does not say whether these are relative or absolute. [15:15]
- Injury definition (Q&A): non-contact injury causing the player to miss a subsequent session or match, in line with the UEFA definition. [20:22] [20:53]
- The 6.8% and 10.5% figures are read from auto captions; they were not checked against the slides.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Directed acyclic graph of ACWR, schedule, session intensity and injury. [11:10]
- Null-model simulation: simulate season-by-season session injuries where only session load matters, then test ACWR against injury with a chi-square test. [13:43] [14:43]
- Adjustment options: survival models, latent variable models, or predicting the upcoming session load as an unmeasured confounder. [18:19] [25:11]
- Comparison of coupled and uncoupled ACWR denominators, same result. [26:42]

## Limits and open questions

- Two teams from two sports; no detail on roster size, number of injuries, or load metric used.
- Details of the real-data adjustment models are "in the paper" and were not shown. [17:49]
- The talk does not show the adjusted effect sizes, only that significance disappears.
- Whether chronic load is protective is explicitly not addressed. [26:42]
- Whether a richer multivariate model finds signal is left open. [23:35]
- The claim that better sensors would make the problem worse is the speaker's intuition, not a test. [21:54]
- The speakers' view that ACWR products are "snake oil" is their own opinion, stated early in the talk. [01:01]
- Wellness questionnaire data: one speaker says across four sports the players mostly enter the same value (captions: "seven") every day. This is his experience, not a study. [24:39]
- Minor inconsistency: the talk opens strongly against the industry but closes saying it has not disproved the literature. [18:49]

## Q&A

- How is injury defined, and are non-training injuries dropped? Non-contact injuries causing a missed session or match; cannot rule out training relation for off-field injuries. [20:22]
- Do device sensitivity limits matter? Noise in load sensors should weaken the effect, so the speaker expects better data not to remove the problem. [21:23]
- How should decision makers avoid snake oil? Much sport science is well supported (nutrition, strength and conditioning); this may not be one of them. [22:33]
- Could wellness, physiological and biomarker data in a multivariate model do better? Possibly; dose is measurable, response is not well measured, and wellness forms lack validation. [23:35] [24:39]
- Can you predict today's load from the prior 7 days? If so, treat it as an unmeasured confounder and adjust; needs statistical skill. [25:11]
- Do high vs low chronic loads differ, and is chronic load protective? Same results using acute load alone; protection not addressed; coupled and uncoupled denominators gave the same results. [26:42]

## Where this applies

- Inference: Any Baylor football dashboard that flags players by ACWR on Catapult player load, or by a similar 7-to-28-day ratio, should be treated as a description of recent load and schedule, not as an injury-risk score. Check whether the flags mostly fire on the same weeks (camp, return from breaks) for every player.
- Inference: When reviewing a non-contact injury, pull that day's planned session load (or the practice script intensity) next to the prior-week ratio before attributing it to "spike" in load. The talk's point is that the current session's intensity may carry the signal.
- Inference: For Baylor's own retrospective analysis, log planned session intensity as a field so injured-session data is not lost. The talk says the injured player's session data is usually thrown out. [17:18]
- Inference: Use the simulation idea as a test of any internal risk model: simulate seasons where only session intensity matters and see whether the model still "finds" an ACWR effect.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: No formal injury-risk model such as ACWR is attributed to Eric in the corpus; ACWR appears only in Clemson reference material. The talk neither conflicts with nor changes a stated Baylor position.
- Eric's baseline: Abrupt, large changes in volume and intensity are treated as an injury-risk driver, and progressions are kept smooth (course material, speaker unconfirmed, tagged Inferred). The talk agrees that load change matters but says the ratio may just reflect the schedule; it leaves open whether spikes themselves cause injury.
- Eric's baseline: Subjective daily wellness surveys were abandoned because athletes learned to give consistent low-effort answers (Explicit, SportSmith piece). The talk agrees: a speaker describes athletes entering the same number every day. [24:39]

## What would have to be true

- Session-level load (planned and actual) for every player and session, including the session where an injury occurs.
- A clear non-contact injury definition (the talk uses missed session or match).
- Enough injuries and seasons at Baylor to fit a model that includes session load; the talk does not give a minimum, and one college roster may be too small.
- Someone with the statistical training to run survival or latent variable models. The speaker says this takes "fair bit" of skill. [25:41]

## Do not apply when

- You would use the talk to say ACWR-style monitoring is useless. The speakers say they did not disprove it, and do not show that chronic load is non-protective. [18:49] [26:42]
- Your data has only a handful of injuries; a null result then says little.
- The injury is contact-related; the talk's definition excludes it.
- You want to generalize from one NFL team and one Italian soccer team to a college football roster with different schedules and session structure.
- The claim is being used as settled in a staff meeting. It is a conference research talk; the adjusted results were not shown.

## First step

Export one season of Catapult session load and injury dates for football, and count how many non-contact injuries had a recorded session load for that day. If the count is near zero, fix the logging before any modeling.

## Summary

The speaker, introduced as director of football research and development for the Tennessee Titans, gives a non-technical walk through building an injury-risk model that staff will actually use. She says to model risk, not individual injuries, and that adoption depends on the front office, scouts, medical staff, coaches, strength coaches and players. She lists data sources (tracking, weight room, speed, player surveys, injury history), scheduling choices, model-design issues such as small samples, and delivery through stoplight thresholds and fast alerts. No model results or accuracy numbers are shown. The talk is a practitioner's checklist and opinion, not a validation study.

## Key claims

- The goal is injury risk, not predicting a specific injury, because risk is actionable and a single injury is hard to predict. [01:01]
- Choose which injuries to model; some (bone breaks, cuts) may be excluded and lower-body injuries may be the priority because they cost more time. [01:32]
- Injury matters for team, player and bottom-line reasons; she cites about 13.2 million per NFL team in injury cash last year. [02:33] [03:06]
- A model will not be used if the front office, scouts, medical staff, coaches, strength coaches and players are not invested. [03:36]
- Telling players why they are tested gives better buy-in and better data. [06:38]
- Data sources: tracking (practice and game), weight-room velocity and power, camera-based form, speed analysis, player self-evaluation, and injury history. [07:08]
- NFL rules bar tracking players outside the building, so sleep, hydration, stress and soreness are hard to capture; a survey is one option, with each player using the scale differently. [08:40] [09:12]
- Injury history is called the greatest predictor of future injury. [09:12]
- Test timing changes meaning: Monday after a game is more a fatigue indicator, Wednesday more a readiness indicator. [10:13]
- Frequent testing causes test fatigue; be selective and cut tests that do not help. [10:43]
- She says the NFL needs three injury models: in-season, offseason and training camp. [11:13]
- Outcome choices include games missed, practices missed, soreness, survey responses, or unsupervised anomaly detection. [12:15]
- Sample size is the big challenge; individual-player models need data, so rookies use position, body-size or skill-group models until an onboarding period yields enough data. [13:15] [14:16]
- Evaluating a working model is hard because success means fewer injuries, and injuries are zero-inflated. [14:16] [14:46]
- Outputs must be interpretable to everyone, use stoplight severity levels, and set reasonable expectations because players cannot always sit. [15:49] [16:19]
- Alerts should be immediate: Monday testing goes out Monday night. [17:21]

## Numbers and definitions

- "Over $400 million in cash" in the NFL on injuries last year, about 13.2 million per team. The captions are garbled ("in cash only in the NFL and injuries") and the year and source are not stated. [02:33]
- Rough timeline: about two years at the Titans; a full season to understand patterns and more than a season to reach predictable mode. [22:31]
- No model accuracy, sample size, variable weights or thresholds are given.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Risk-not-prediction framing; injury type and location filtering. [01:01] [01:32]
- Data pipeline: tracking data, weight-room, speed, survey, injury history. [07:08]
- Three seasonal models (in-season, offseason, training camp). [11:13]
- Group-level model for new players, then individual model after onboarding. [14:16]
- Stoplight (green, amber, red) severity thresholds. [16:19]
- Central data warehouse, API use, or a simple SQL Server (she says she is not a data engineer). [20:28] [20:59]

## Limits and open questions

- No results, no validation, no sample sizes, no model type named.
- She says how to tell whether the model works is hard and does not resolve it. [14:16]
- The claim about injury history and the usefulness of "a good force plate" and hamstring tester are her statements with no source. [09:12] [23:34]
- Her claim that surveys differ by player (scale use) is given without data. [09:12]
- Employer view: presented by a Titans staff member; the dollar figure and practices reflect the club's perspective.
- Captions garble the host's intro ("ker also known as craft analytics group"), and the host's stated title differs slightly from the video title.

## Q&A

- How to decide on adopting new tech or a metric, and communicating to athletes who feel like guinea pigs? Testing fatigue produces bad data; start from research and other sports, tell players the reason, test infrequently, and drop what does not work. [18:55] [19:26] [20:28]
- How to store and consolidate data? Central warehouse, APIs, or a simple SQL Server; she is not a data engineer. [20:28] [20:59]
- Internal models versus external research? External work is inspiration; thresholds from soccer may not apply to the NFL; most work is internal. [21:30] [22:01]
- How long did data discovery take? About two years and still refining; coaching changes reset schedules; a full season to see patterns. [22:31]
- Which data has priority? Tracking data first for workload; then strength coach input; force plates and hamstring testers have proven ability to show risk (her words). [23:04] [23:34]
- Risk or prediction, which do stakeholders value? Risk; a date-specific prediction gives coaches nothing to do. [24:06] [25:09]

type: video-summary

title: "SSAC26: Heat Safety in Professional Sport: Aligning Data Physiology and Policy"
event: SSAC26 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [David Martin]
topics: [american-football, sports-science, injury-health, policy, competitive-advantage]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft

## Summary

The speaker, introduced as director of science at Perry Weather, argues that exertional heat illness is preventable and that wet bulb globe temperature (WBGT) monitoring can guide when teams practice, how they acclimatize and what conditions to prepare for. He reviews heat stroke deaths in football, heat acclimation physiology, policy changes in Georgia, and his own look at historical WBGT data from NFL stadium sensors. He also reports a penalty-count difference when WBGT was above 60 F. The company sells environmental monitoring hardware, which he discloses, and the penalty analysis is preliminary.

## Key claims

- Exertional heat stroke is still the leading preventable cause of death in sport. [02:03] [02:33]
- Heat degrades aerobic performance and raises core temperature and heart rate; chronic exposure builds resilience. [02:03]
- Among 61 heat stroke fatalities in one study, all occurred in conditioning drills and not games, most were linemen. [03:35]
- Mapping cases by WBGT lets organizations build policy and best practice. [04:05]

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: For football, conditioning Goal 1 is alactic and aerobic capacity for fall-camp demands, with glycolytic work absorbed through camp (Explicit). The talk extends this by adding an environmental constraint: camp conditioning carries the heat risk.
- Eric's baseline: Abrupt changes in load are treated as an injury-risk driver (tagged Inferred). The talk's August return-from-summer risk is consistent, but it gives no load metric.

## What would have to be true

- WBGT sensors (or access to a local station) at each practice location, read on a fixed schedule.
- A written modification policy from Athletic Medicine that names who can change practice and at which thresholds.
- A way to compare core temperature or proxy measures; the talk uses chamber core temperature, which practice does not provide.
